title: Caroline Flack: recovered headline sample

researchScope.method: Fixed dated sample from publisher, court and inquiry sources. The public GET audit corrected accessible title/date metadata, dropped unrelated redirects and unsupported 404/PDF rows, and labelled previously recovered records with current 403/request errors. Reproductions and updated pages are clearly distinguished. This is not a census.
limitations: The sample is event-led and uneven: accessible records cluster around the charge, court appearance, host replacement, and late-January social-media dispute. It cannot establish daily or weekly volume growth.

The Guardian's separate analysis reported 387 UK national-newspaper print stories mentioning Flack between 2019-08-14 and 2020-02-14, including 99 in The Sun. Those are aggregate counts, not this sample; the Guardian does not provide a daily series or itemized corpus in the article, and the 99 must not be treated as daily volume, 99 negative stories, or a recoverable list of 99 unique Sun headlines.

The Sun Valentine-card story was reported as published online on 2020-02-14 and later removed/replaced. The exact original article URL was not recovered, so originalURL is null and the headline is attributed only as a reproduced quotation.

aggregateContext.unit: print stories in which Caroline Flack appeared in headline or body, as reported by The Guardian

auditMethod.unit: One distinct publisher URL / one item, not one mention or story event.
auditMethod.deduplication: Canonicalize URLs and remove exact URL duplicates; flag cross-outlet reprints/syndications for review.
auditMethod.dateRule: Use first publication/edition date from the publisher or dated archive. Do not substitute last-modified time, event date, or retrospective publication date.
auditMethod.headlineRule: Quote exact publisher headline where accessible. Label archive reproductions. Exclude captions/summary wording from exact headline count.

researchScope.windowCaveat: Fixed window 2019-12-12 through 2020-02-14 inclusive; 24 dated rows remain after audit. Two Reddit-only rows and items without adequate support are excluded. A reproduced Sun online headline is retained with its updated secondary-page metadata mismatch stated. The separate 99 Sun print-story aggregate has no daily series.

waveAssessment.finding: This recovered sample can show event-linked clusters in the retrievable headlines, especially 13–23 December, then isolated January coverage and the 14 February card story. It cannot calculate when total volume grew, quantify the growth, or prove a wave from the aggregate 99 count.

candidateWaves.sampleObservation: Charge reports appear on 13 and again on 16–17 December; by 17 December several outlets report Flack stepping down. This is clear event-linked repetition in the sample, but not a daily volume curve.

Replacement coverage on 20–21 December is followed by court-day reports on 23 December and the Christmas social-media reports on 24–25 December. This recovered sample shows event-linked repetition, not whether total output peaked then.

The reproduced Sun New Year’s Day edition headline/photo and LBC follow-up form a discrete attention-spike candidate after the first hearing. New Year’s Eve references may describe advance availability, not the 1 January edition date; there is no day-by-day denominator.
Multiple reports revisit the relationship and split rumours on one day; the Independent documents Flack's objection to gossip. This suggests recurrence, not a sustained volume trend.
A separate Sun online card story was published on the final day of the Guardian print-analysis window. The online publication is not confirmed as one of the 99 Sun print stories.

criteria.public_value: Did the item explain a matter of legitimate public interest (the charge, court process, employment decision, or institutional response), or mainly exploit celebrity attention?
criteria.context: Did it distinguish arrest, charge, allegation, plea, evidence and verdict; include the denial/not-guilty status; and avoid presenting contested prosecution claims as established facts?
criteria.framing: Did its headline and imagery add relevant information, or sensationalize, ridicule, sexualize, or imply guilt beyond what was established?
criteria.care: Did it account for privacy, vulnerability, distress and foreseeable impact, especially around highly personal or graphic material?
criteria.consistency: Did it use the same evidential standards and fairness given to comparable people/cases, including when the subject was a famous woman and when the story later became criticism of the press?
criteria.transparency: Did it name sources, separate fact from allegation, seek or clearly report a response, and explain corrections, removal or changed context?

observations.observation: The charge, stepdown, replacement and plea had public relevance because they changed a national television programme and involved court proceedings. Repeated celebrity/relationship updates and a mocking card offered weaker public-interest justification in the sampled headlines.

ITV's 17 December report included Flack's statement that matters were not as reported; several court reports explicitly recorded the not-guilty plea and Burton's position. Headlines using 'lamp' or vivid court imagery could nevertheless make a disputed account feel settled. No verdict is in this corpus.

Neutral procedural formulations coexist with wordplay ('Caroline whack!'), 'lover' language, 'denies ... with lamp', and 'bedroom bloodbath'. These choices shift attention from the limited procedural fact to culpability, intimacy or spectacle.

The 25 December headline repeats Flack's own statement of strain, while 30 January records her objection to gossip. The reproduced Sun bedroom image/headline and Valentine-card headline raise sharper privacy and dignity concerns. This review makes no claim that any individual item caused her death.

This small, single-subject sample cannot support a matched-case comparison. The Guardian's aggregate finds 99 Sun print mentions and reports tone categories, but that method does not establish a daily curve or whether every sampled online item belonged to the print corpus.

Publisher pages provide strong traceability for mainstream reports. The removed Sun card story and recovered Sun front-page wording rely on later reproductions, so the original article text, URL, corrections and full contemporaneous context remain unavailable here.

rolePlayedOutletDefences.outlet: The Sun (role-play, not an actual statement)
rolePlayedOutletDefences.basis: Reproduced Sun headlines in later reporting and the Guardian's aggregate analysis.
rolePlayedOutletDefences.text: We reported on an arrest and a court case involving a presenter at the centre of a major television programme. The charge, the court hearing and her departure from Love Island were matters readers were already following. We would say that the New Year photograph was part of reporting what the court had heard, and that the Valentine card was a newsworthy example of the public conversation around the case. We should still answer whether the image and joke added necessary information, whether their presentation implied guilt, and whether we gave Flack a fair chance to respond.

rolePlayedOutletDefences.outlet: The Independent (role-play, not an actual statement)
rolePlayedOutletDefences.basis: Sampled Independent reports include Burton's response, the stepdown, plea, Christmas post and January objection to gossip.
rolePlayedOutletDefences.text: We covered the legal process and the consequences for Love Island, and we reported both the not-guilty plea and Burton's public support. We also covered Flack's own words when she said she had a story to tell and later objected to her family's life becoming entertainment. We would defend those as relevant updates, while reviewing whether reporting repeatedly on relationship rumours enlarged the very gossip she was asking the press to stop.

rolePlayedOutletDefences.outlet: ITV News (role-play, not an actual statement)
rolePlayedOutletDefences.basis: Sampled ITV items report the charge, stepdown and scheduled court appearance.
rolePlayedOutletDefences.text: We reported on a presenter who worked on our programme, the change in the winter series, and a public court appearance. Our 17 December report included Flack's statement that matters were not as reported and quoted ITV's decision to remain in contact. We would say the audience needed clear information about who would host the show. We should also acknowledge the institutional relationship and take care that programme news does not crowd out her stated position or turn a legal allegation into a programme promotion.

rolePlayedOutletDefences.outlet: The Guardian (role-play, not an actual statement)
rolePlayedOutletDefences.basis: Sampled Guardian reports cover the charge, host replacement and subsequent aggregate analysis of print coverage.
rolePlayedOutletDefences.text: We reported the charge as a charge, then the decision to replace the host, and later examined the scale and tone of newspaper coverage. Our later analysis stated its limits: the sample was not definitive, and neutral stories formed the majority. We would defend scrutiny of both the legal story and press treatment as public-interest reporting. We should keep the 99 Sun print mentions separate from online items and avoid suggesting that a count or tone classification proves causation.
